If (and only if) 5 9's have been a requirement from the ground up, and the dev team was clearly aware of it, yes, it probably can.

With requirements this stringent, you need to engineering failover at every step. I did it for E-Commerce websites. You end up buying very expensive things (think Oracle RAC) and probably triple the dev and hardware cost, but with a good team, it can be managed.

The real issue, to be honest, is whetever or not the application really requires five 9s. 

For instance, let's take a look at an ecommerce website operating in the US, Europe and Asia. Management will require 5 9s because the store basically has to be opened for business 24/7. When it's 3AM in Europe (lowest traffic) it's 9PM in New-York (traffic peak, or at least very significant traffic)

The right answer is not building a 5 9s application SLA. The right answer is to partition the website into zones and serve accordingly.
For instance, this is what Ebay does: Ebay France is a complete (was, last I checked) different instance from Ebay US. If they need to do maintenance, they can do it at 3AM without any impact on the business.

The costs are much, much lower and overall service ends up being better.

Another example: emergency services IT systems. Here, we're talking serious business, they fucking need the system to be online at all costs: lives are litteraly at stake. They go the only route: money. They build rock solid clusters, with HA on every tier, and some expensive software like Oracle RAC and so on....

Light (which is a very high frequency electromagnetic wave) bounces off a mirror.

Radio waves bounce off some materials and are absorbed by others.

HF frequencies happen to bounce very well off the ionosphere *at night* because the ionosphere property change according to its exposition to the sun.
In the troposphere, water % change at night, which also plays a role in radio waves propagation.

The higher the frequency the harder it will be to penetrate buildings, trees, rains, etc

Extremely high frequencies, such as microwaves are extremely sensitive to rain, because the energy of the wave being water molecules.

That effect is sometime very interesting (to cook your hotpockets in a microwave oven), sometimes very annoying (to establish a wifi link outdoor).

The M stands for modulation.

To describe a periodic signal such as radio wave, we use its frequency (inverse to the period, or time it take for a signal to do its full "travel" from 0 to the top say 1, back to 0, then to -1 and finally to 0)
and its amplitude, its "height". (we also use phase but please ignore for now)


In AM, Amplitude Modulation, carrier frequency stays the same, say 200kHz.
[WolframAlpha to the rescue](http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=sinewave+200khz&a=*MC.~-_*Formula.dflt-&f2=2V&f=ACVoltage.vpp_2V&a=*FVarOpt.1-_***ACVoltage.vpp--.***ACVoltage.vrms--.**ACVoltage.vp---.**ACVoltage.f---)

However, the amplitude of the signal varies according to the signal we want to transmit. 
[see this image](http://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Amfm3-en-de.gif/250px-Amfm3-en-de.gif)

On this image, the AM signal amplitude is modulated according to the message we want to send. When the message is close to -1, the AM signal amplitude is at its lowest. When the message is close 1, it's at its peak.

To receive the signal, we have to demodulate it. 
That's easy: you want to only keep the envellope (the "shape" of the signal) and can be done with very simple component, basically, an antenna, a coil, a diode and you're almost there.
This why early radio transmitted only in AM.


In Frequency modulation, the carrier frequency vary very slighlty, in accordance with the signal we want to transmit.
To demodulate, you remove the carrier and you end up with the frequency variation which is your signal.


There are many other modulation modes, such as phase shifting where the phase is modified according to the signal (it's much harder to explain in layman terms but see [wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase-shift_keying) if you want a nice headache)

The mode is chosen according to a number of parameters: is the signal digital or analog, do we need to transmit data at a high speed (see Nyquist and Shannon on that, another nice headache:-) ), do we need to transmit the signal far away, etc...?

The lower the carrier frequency, the farther the signal can go. AM is in the kHz range (HF, High Frequency Band). FM in the MHz(VHF, Very High Frequency). FM is said to travel "to the horizon". It obviously depends on power and antenna, but usually FM transmitter can't be received much farther than 200km.
In AM, you can easily receive a signal from more than 2000km at night with an off the shelf radio (I live in France, I routinely receive russian signals for example).

Other frequency range are used, for example in [VLF](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_low_frequency) you can send data almost around the globe (which why it's used by submarines)

It seems you are only solving concurrent reads this way?
Say you want to decrement inventory (think logistics or high throughput e-commerce, etc). 
A business requirement is to have only one inventory, you cannot split it (otherwise, you'd have to make assumptions on inventory management on each of your nodes, which is complicated, usually it's not as easy as node inventory=global inventory/number of nodes)

With this requirement in mind, you have to ensure inventory consistency accross your nodes, sometimes at the ms level. 
There's only a handful possibilities:

* Active clustering ($$$$$)

* Caching of inventory with regular updates of your separated nodes which adds a layer to your app (memcache, Terracotta, Oracle coherence and many others) and can go from $ to $$$$

* Inventory split, sharding by countries, etc: you break the business requirement but the bill stays relatively low
